title: Semicolons, colons, dashes and parentheses
note: A semicolon joins two closely related independent clauses, including before a conjunctive adverb such as however, and separates list items that already contain commas. A colon follows a complete clause to introduce a list, an explanation or a quotation. Dashes set material off with emphasis; parentheses set it off quietly.

items.a: links independent clauses or divides complex list items
d: introduces a list after a complete clause

d: joins two clauses that contrast with 'but'

read.title: Three ways to join two thoughts
text: Suppose you have two complete sentences that belong together: "The museum closed early. A storm was coming." You can leave them as two sentences. You can join them with a comma and a coordinating conjunction: "The museum closed early, for a storm was coming." Or you can use a semicolon, which signals that the clauses are equal partners: "The museum closed early; a storm was coming." What you may not do is join them with a bare comma, which creates a comma splice.

The colon does a more specific job. It says that what follows will explain, list or illustrate what came before: "The museum closed early for one reason: a storm was coming." The words before a colon must form a complete clause. "The reasons were: wind and rain" breaks this rule, since "The reasons were" cannot stand alone.

Dashes and parentheses both interrupt a sentence, but with opposite tones. A dash raises its voice—look at this. Parentheses lower theirs (a quiet aside). Choose the mark that matches how loudly you want the extra material to speak.

q.q: Which joins the two sentences correctly?
o: The museum closed early, a storm was coming.
The museum closed early; a storm was coming.
The museum closed early: and a storm was coming.

q.q: Why is "The reasons were: wind and rain" faulty?
o: The words before the colon are not a complete clause
A colon can never introduce a list
It needs a semicolon after rain

q.q: According to the reading, how do dashes differ from parentheses?
o: Dashes emphasize; parentheses play material down
